title: MODEL OF AN ELECTRONIC VOTING SCHEME WITH THE POSSIBILITY OF CHANGING THE PARTICIPANT'S DECISION BEFORE THE END OF VOTING
abstract: Существующие протоколы электронного голосования, как правило, обладают архитектурой, в которой отправка бюллетеня является необратимым действием. Такой подход ограничивает удобство использования системы, поскольку участник не может исправить случайную ошибку или изменить свое решение в течение периода голосования без прохождения повторной процедуры аутентификации либо аннулирования ранее поданного бюллетеня. Целью настоящей работы является разработка теоретической модели криптографического протокола электронного голосования, обеспечивающей нативную возможность многократного изменения решения для повышения удобства использования при сохранении анонимности и корректности подсчета. Архитектура предлагаемой модели основана на совместном использовании схемы обязательств с потайным входом для реализации свойства изменения решения, проверяемой случайной функции (VRF) для формирования бюллетеней, протокола Privacy Pass для анонимной авторизации участников и смешанных сетей (Mix-Nets), обеспечивающих сокрытие связи между пользователем и передаваемыми сообщениями. Разработан протокол электронного голосования, позволяющий участнику неоднократно изменять свое решение без повторного обращения к центру регистрации после получения права на участие в голосовании, что уменьшает количество интерактивных действий и повышает удобство использования системы. Проведен теоретический анализ стойкости предложенной модели, подтверждающий выполнение основных и ряда расширенных свойств, включая, полноту, устойчивость, приемлемость, проверяемость, конфиденциальность участника, одноразовость, справедливость, атомарную и универсальную проверяемость, а также возможность изменения решения. Благодаря модульной архитектуре модель допускает применение различных криптографических примитивов, включая постквантовые алгоритмы, без изменения общей логики функционирования протокола, что делает предложенный подход перспективной основой для построения защищенных систем электронного голосования, стойких к атакам квантового компьютера.

title: Hidden relationships in a document-derived property graph: top-k chunk embeddings and inverse-distance weighting over a dynamically evolving ontology
abstract: Large language models extracting knowledge graphs from text capture only explicitly stated facts, often leaving semantically related entities disconnected across documents. We present an additive, engine-neutral second pass that discovers these latent ties without altering extracted facts. Each document is chunked and embedded once; top-k nearest- neighbor queries across existing chunks yield candidate node pairs via entity membership maps. Candidate pairs are scored using Shepard inverse-distance weighting with a rescaled chord distance metric, avoiding the threshold-collapsing flaw of affine cosine scoring behind a k-NN gate. Un-gated per-pair accumulators form a commutative monoid, ensuring the pipeline is strictly order-independent and scales incrementally without recomputing prior documents. Implemented across FalkorDB, Kinetica, ArangoDB, and Neo4j, our method shows that 768- and 240-dimensional embeddings retain 92% and 72% edge fidelity against a 3072-D baseline while achieving a 25x faster top-k formulation.

title: Strengthening LargeRDFBench for Interoperable Federated SPARQL Evaluation
abstract: LargeRDFBench is one of the most comprehensive benchmarks for evaluating federated SPARQL query engines, combining real, interlinked datasets with a rich query suite that has made it a reference point for the community. Evaluations of federated engines are published by comparing engine results against the benchmark's expected results, so those expected results must themselves be reproducible. Moreover, several of its data dumps violate the RDF specifications, so only engines that parse RDF leniently can host them, and its expected results are distributed in an ad hoc format. We identify, categorize and repair these data-quality issues with a reproducible cleaning pipeline, producing standards-conformant serializations of every affected dataset. Furthermore, we re-encode the benchmark's expected results in the W3C SPARQL 1.1 Query Results JSON Format and correct their discrepancies. Every dataset now parses under strict RDF parsers, and the expected results are machine-verifiable through a standard format, extending the benchmark's reach to the full range of conformant engines while staying faithful to the original data. Reproducing the expected results end-to-end with an independent implementation uncovers corruption in the published reference, and discrepancies between our results and the original ones, some not trivial to resolve, others open questions. We further perform a preliminary comparison, not previously explored, of ASK- and COUNT-based source selection in the FedX algorithm. This work strengthens an already valuable community resource by aligning its artifacts with the RDF standards, broadening the set of engines that can be fairly and reproducibly compared. We also raise the question of how the results of federated queries under automatic source selection can be made reproducible.

title: Tail-Replay: Escaping the Curse of Linear Attention in Prefix Caching for Hybrid LLMs
abstract: Hybrid large language models interleave full-attention layers with linear-attention layers to reduce the cost of long-context inference. This structure complicates prefix caching: full-attention key-value caches are token-addressable, whereas linear-attention layers maintain recurrent states that cannot be rolled back to arbitrary prefix boundaries. Existing hybrid prefix caching methods address this mismatch by storing recurrent-state checkpoints. As a result, token-level matches are directly usable only at positions aligned with stored checkpoints, constraining prefix reuse to a discrete set of boundaries. We present Tail-Replay, a prefix caching mechanism that enables unconstrained token-level prefix reuse in hybrid large language models. The key insight is that linear-attention mechanisms such as Gated DeltaNet can be viewed as a structured, lossy compression of the input prefix: gated recurrent updates progressively attenuate the contributions of earlier inputs. Consequently, the recurrent state of a matched prefix can be well approximated by replaying only a short, recent suffix of that prefix. Tail-Replay exploits this property by caching the exact full-attention key-value cache while omitting recurrent-state checkpoints. On a cache hit, it reconstructs the linear-attention states by replaying a short, recent suffix of the matched prefix. As a result, the reuse boundary is determined by the shared tokens rather than by recurrent-state checkpoints. We evaluate Tail-Replay on three Gated DeltaNet-based hybrid models using the LongBench and RULER benchmarks. With only a 5--10\% replay budget, it retains 92.8--99.9\% of full-prefill quality on LongBench and RULER. For serving efficiency, we evaluate time-to-first-token speedups across multiple matched-prefix lengths---8K, 16K, and 32K. The speedup grows with prefix length, reaching $9.1$--$14.3\times$ over full prefill at 32K.

title: Opening the Black Box: An Exactly Solvable Neural Network
abstract: Associative memory and sequence modelling are two foundational problems in machine learning and computational neuroscience, underlying capabilities from content-addressable recall to the long-range sequence processing at the core of modern large language models. The dominant architectures, classical and modern Hopfield networks for memory, transformers and state-space models (SSMs) for sequences, perform strongly but resist analysis: their computations are defined through implicit recurrent updates or all-pairs attention. They are understood largely through post hoc, empirical interpretability rather than first principles. This thesis addresses the resulting transparency gap by developing models whose computation admits an exact, closed-form description. The unifying object is a complex-valued nonlinear oscillator network, a complex generalization of the Kuramoto model, rendered exactly solvable by a nonlinear coordinate transformation that yields the closed-form propagator x(t) = exp(Kt)x(0). This single operator is used in three studies. First, an exactly solvable associative memory encodes patterns as eigenmodes of a complex connectivity matrix obtained by QR factorization; recall becomes a complex-walk filtration that reconstructs occluded inputs through phase-coherent interference, free of spurious attractors, and outperforms modern Hopfield networks on occluded-MNIST completion and generalization to unseen digits. Second, a formal correspondence is established between diagonal linear time-invariant SSMs and the oscillator network, embedding the SSM into a ring topology whose latent state superposes travelling waves; via a Carleman embedding of the GELU nonlinearity, an exact end-to-end operator is derived for the forward pass of S4, a second-order truncation recovering roughly 94% of classification performance on a real-world task. Third, a new architecture, S1, derives its nonlinear readout from the linearizing transformation, so the entire computation is a closed-form operator parameterized by the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of K; S1 attains competitive accuracy on several benchmarks and supports causal control through targeted modal intervention. Together, these show that recall and sequence processing are two regimes of one operator, memory as the truncated walk-order expansion of exp(Kt), sequence processing as the same propagator sampled in discrete time, distinguished by the spectrum of K. Mathematical transparency and competitive performance are thus compatible, with implications for trustworthy sequence models in high-stakes domains.

title: A Systematic Review of Relation Extraction for Various Indian and Non-Indian Languages
abstract: Abstract This article comprehensively reviews text relation extraction for various Indian and non-Indian languages. The study involves a comparative investigation of diverse models developed using machine learning (ML) & deep learning (DL) approach for relation extraction. A detailed literature review has been conducted for diverse Indian and non-Indian languages. The comparative study focuses on the effectiveness of diverse models across these languages. This paper highlights the strengths and limitations of various approaches, providing insights into the best practices for relation extraction in diverse linguistic contexts.

title: Minos: apparatus, parser and per-case captures for "Capable but Counted Out: Harness-Induced Bias in Tool-Use Evaluation of Open-Weight Large Language Models"
abstract: The complete artifact behind the study of harness-induced bias in tool-use evaluation of open-weight large language models: the benchmark apparatus, the model-agnostic multi-dialect call parser, the scorers, every analysis and figure script, and the raw per-case capture logs. The study follows a run-once, re-parse-many design: each (model, case) pair was run once per delivery mode and each captured raw output re-scored offline under every parser condition. Every number reported in the paper is therefore re-derivable from the released captures with no model access and no GPU. scripts/audit_paper_claims.py re-derives and checks all 141 headline claims in one command. Contents. 19 open-weight models (3B-14B) plus two held-out sets, benchmarked on three BFCL categories and an evaluation set derived from the ToolACE data, under two tool-delivery modes and three parser conditions; a 300-case generated format-stress set; a 15-task multi-turn agentic suite; and the fp16 end-to-end validation runs. Licensing. Software is MIT (see LICENSE); the capture logs, result notes, figures and task definitions are CC BY 4.0 (see LICENSE-DATA). Third-party inputs are not redistributed. The BFCL case files, the ToolACE corpus and the model tokenizers keep their own terms and are fetched from their own sources at pinned revisions by scripts/fetch_data.py, then verified against a checksum manifest. See data/README.md. Three of the tokenizers are for gated models whose licences forbid redistribution; that access barrier is itself a reported result. Redaction. The captures are the models' raw text, with one exception. In mult_native.jsonl (case multiple_61, deepseek-coder-v2-lite) the model invented a Google Custom Search call and emitted a well-formed Google API key as the key argument. Whether it synthesised that string or reproduced one memorised from training data cannot be told from the output, so the value is replaced with REDACTED_GOOGLE_API_KEY. The case already scored a miss in every condition, so no reported number depends on it and scripts/audit_paper_claims.py still reproduces all 141 claims. Start from REPRODUCE.md.

title: Quantum Information Entropy Mapping
abstract: Quantum information entropy, a fundamental quantity in quantum information theory, presents a significant challenge in practical applications due to its inherent sensitivity to noise and imperfections. This paper introduces a novel quantum information entropy mapping technique, aiming to bridge the gap between classical entropy and quantum information entropy. We propose a method leveraging topological structures to induce non-linear mappings, allowing for optimization of compression and encryption processes. The core claim is that this mapping enables efficient quantum data compression and encryption through the influence of topological principles. This work explores the potential of this approach to address limitations of existing methods and opens avenues for advanced quantum data processing.

title: Graph-Based Representations of Semantic Networks for Knowledge Discovery
abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to knowledge discovery leveraging graph-based representations of semantic networks. Traditional methods for analyzing semantic networks often suffer from scalability issues and computational complexity, particularly when dealing with large and intricate knowledge bases. Our system automatically constructs a graph representation from a given semantic network, facilitating efficient querying, reasoning, and ultimately, knowledge discovery. The core of the approach lies in transforming the network's inherent relationships into a graph structure, where nodes represent entities and edges represent semantic connections. This transformation enables the application of graph algorithms optimized for relationship analysis, significantly reducing computational overhead. The resulting graph representation allows for the identification of patterns, clusters, and anomalies within the knowledge base that might be missed by conventional methods. We demonstrate the potential of this approach through a theoretical framework and outline key considerations for implementation. The system's scalability and efficiency are central to its value proposition, offering a viable solution for knowledge discovery in increasingly complex and expansive knowledge domains. The primary goal is to provide a more effective and manageable way to explore and understand interconnected data.

title: Decentralized Federated Reinforcement Learning with Multi-Agent Credit Assignment
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to decentralized federated reinforcement learning (DFRL) that tackles the critical challenge of multi-agent credit assignment. Traditional multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) struggles to scale effectively in decentralized settings due to the difficulty in determining which agents are responsible for the overall reward. Our method introduces a decentralized credit assignment algorithm leveraging Shapley values, providing a fair and efficient mechanism for distributing rewards among agents. Combined with a communication protocol, this architecture enables scalable and robust learning across multiple agents operating independently. The core claim is that innovative credit assignment solutions are necessary to scale MARL in decentralized environments. This work offers a foundational framework for developing more practical and effective DFRL systems.

title: High-Order Quantum Phase Transition Algorithm
abstract: This paper introduces a novel high-order quantum phase transition algorithm designed to precisely simulate and control quantum phase transitions. Traditional approaches often struggle with the complexity of these transitions, limiting their applicability to materials optimization and design. This algorithm leverages a sophisticated quantum simulation framework and advanced operations to achieve accurate modeling and control, offering a significant advancement in this field. The core mechanism centers around a dynamic quantum state evolution, guided by a tailored control scheme, facilitating the exploration of multiple phase transitions simultaneously. We present a comprehensive theoretical framework and demonstrate the algorithm's effectiveness through a series of applied examples, showcasing its potential for rapid and accurate material design. The algorithm's focus is on enhancing the ability to predict and manipulate phase transitions, thereby unlocking new possibilities in materials science.

title: Title: Hierarchical Geometric Modeling for Neural Network Interpretability
abstract: Neural networks are increasingly deployed in various applications, but their complex internal representations often hinder interpretability. This paper proposes a novel hierarchical geometric modeling approach to decompose neural network activations into smaller, more understandable components. We develop a nested model structure, where each level represents a simpler geometric abstraction. This allows us to analyze the network's decision-making process through the lens of geometric intuition, offering a potential pathway toward improved model transparency and explainability. The core mechanism involves constructing a hierarchical model, progressively simplifying the network's representation. This framework will be tested with a variety of neural network architectures, and the results will demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach in identifying key factors influencing network behavior.

title: Title: Emergent Information Coding via Modular Neural Networks
abstract: This paper explores the potential of modular neural networks to achieve self-organization and distributed intelligence. Traditional neural networks are often viewed as deterministic, limiting their ability to exhibit complex, adaptive behavior. We propose a novel architecture – modular neural networks – that leverages interconnected units to encode and propagate information through a system of communication and exchange, fostering emergent behavior without explicit control. The core mechanism centers around the design of modular units that dynamically adapt and communicate, enabling the network to spontaneously reorganize itself. This approach moves beyond the limitations of traditional deep learning by introducing a fundamental shift in how information is processed and represented. We present preliminary results demonstrating the emergence of complex patterns and functionalities within a modular network, suggesting a paradigm shift towards more robust and adaptable AI systems.

title: Title: Dynamic Constraint Feedback Loops in Evolutionary Algorithms
abstract: Evolutionary algorithms have proven effective in solving complex optimization problems, but often struggle with finding optimal solutions, particularly in dynamic and uncertain environments. This paper introduces a novel evolutionary algorithm that leverages dynamic constraint feedback loops to actively shape the evolution of constraints. We propose a mechanism for continuous monitoring of algorithm performance and adaptive constraint adjustment based on the outcomes of previous iterations. This approach aims to enhance the algorithm's ability to navigate complex landscapes and discover optimal solutions more efficiently. The core claim is that this dynamic constraint feedback loop significantly improves the effectiveness of evolutionary algorithms by integrating feedback.

title: Dynamic Topology Learning for Graph Neural Networks
abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have demonstrated remarkable success in various graph-related tasks, including node classification, link prediction, and graph classification. However, traditional GNNs often rely on fixed graph structures, which may not effectively capture the underlying complex relationships within the data. This paper proposes a novel framework for Dynamic Topology Learning (DTL) for GNNs, aiming to address this limitation. The core idea is to enable the GNN to dynamically adapt its graph topology during training, allowing it to better align with the data's inherent structure and the specific task requirements. This is achieved through a mechanism that introduces the ability to modify the graph structure, such as adding or removing edges, based on the learned representations and the current task demands. The proposed DTL framework is expected to improve both the performance and robustness of GNNs.

title: Distributed Differential Privacy via Graph-Based Correlation Learning
abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to achieving stronger differential privacy guarantees in distributed machine learning settings. The core idea centers around leveraging the inherent correlations between data points within a distributed network, represented as a graph. We propose utilizing a Graph Neural Network (GNN) to learn a "correlation embedding" that explicitly models these relationships. This embedding is then used to refine the privacy protection applied during model updates, effectively masking individual contributions while maintaining the overall accuracy of the learning process. Our method represents a significant departure from traditional aggregation techniques, offering a more nuanced and adaptive approach to privacy preservation in the face of complex data dependencies. We demonstrate the potential for improved privacy bounds and accuracy through theoretical analysis and illustrate the concept with a conceptual framework. This approach provides a pathway towards more robust and practical distributed machine learning systems where privacy and utility are effectively balanced.

title: Title: Universal Quantum State Representation via Fractal Geometry
abstract: This paper investigates the potential of utilizing fractal geometry to represent quantum states, aiming to overcome limitations of existing encoding schemes. The core claim is that a novel representation based on fractal patterns can facilitate efficient encoding and manipulation of quantum states, specifically by enabling the representation of complex correlations. We explore the mathematical foundations of this approach, detailing the design of a fractal structure and its associated properties. The paper presents preliminary results demonstrating the capacity for encoding and manipulating quantum states using this framework, offering a potential advancement in quantum information theory. Keywords: Quantum State Representation, Fractal Geometry, Quantum Entanglement, Information Theory, Representation Theory.

title: Quantum Entanglement Non-Asymmetry Computation – Topological Information Coding
abstract: Quantum entanglement forms the bedrock of quantum computing, offering unique capabilities for computation and communication. This paper investigates a novel non-asymmetric computation framework predicated on the manipulation of entangled states, aiming to unlock its potential for information encoding and processing. We propose a computational model centered around the exploitation of entanglement's inherent asymmetries, designing algorithms to leverage these properties for data manipulation and computation. Our work explores the theoretical implications of this approach, highlighting the potential for achieving significant advancements in quantum information processing. Specifically, this research investigates the feasibility of utilizing entangled states to perform complex calculations and offers a preliminary assessment of the framework's potential for quantum algorithms. The core claim is that this approach offers a distinct path toward quantum computing, leveraging the unique properties of entanglement.

title: Nonlinear Topological Geometry: A Dynamic Self-Organizing Theory
abstract: This paper explores the application of dynamic topology and quantum field theory to the design of an algorithm capable of autonomously identifying and manipulating complex system topological structures. We propose a novel approach leveraging a quantum-entangled topology "graph" model, dynamically associating quantum states with topological structures. This system utilizes quantum algorithms to achieve adaptive energy conservation and information transfer. Traditional topological approaches often lack the ability to dynamically adjust and optimize complex systems, a significant limitation in real-world applications. This work aims to address this limitation by introducing a novel framework that facilitates self-organizing topological structures through quantum entanglement and optimization.

title: Black-headed Spider Monkey Metaheuristic Algorithm Inspired by Foraging Behavior
abstract: This paper proposes a novel metaheuristic algorithm, termed the Black-headed Spider Monkey Metaheuristic Algorithm (BSMMA), inspired by the foraging behavior of black-headed spider monkeys. These monkeys exhibit complex strategies for food acquisition, including exploration, exploitation, and adaptive movement patterns. The BSMMA leverages these observed behaviors to develop a new optimization process. The algorithm utilizes a population-based approach, incorporating elements of Lévy flight, adaptive step size adjustment, and a dynamic exploration-exploitation balance. The core of the algorithm is a 'hunting' mechanism mimicking the spider monkey's search for food, where individuals move strategically through the search space, adjusting their movement based on food density estimations. The performance of the BSMMA is evaluated on a range of benchmark optimization problems, demonstrating its effectiveness in finding near-optimal solutions within reasonable computational time. The algorithm's adaptability and robustness are highlighted, and future research directions are discussed. The primary objective is to provide a robust and efficient optimization method drawing inspiration from the intricate foraging strategies of a fascinating primate. The algorithm's key parameters are designed to reflect the adaptive nature observed in spider monkey behavior. The results show that BSMMA can outperform traditional metaheuristic algorithms in certain problem landscapes.

title: Title: Quantum Entanglement-Driven Chaos Simulation
abstract: Quantum entanglement, a phenomenon where two or more particles become linked and share the same fate, presents a revolutionary approach to simulating complex systems, particularly chaotic dynamics. This research explores the potential of leveraging entanglement to create a novel simulation technique, aiming to achieve more stable and predictable chaos behavior than currently employed methods. The core mechanism centers around designing a highly sophisticated entanglement algorithm that actively monitors and manipulates entanglement states, introducing carefully controlled decoherence events to induce specific chaotic dynamics. This paper details the design of such an algorithm, its underlying principles, and the potential implications for understanding and, potentially, controlling chaotic systems. We present a framework for generating and analyzing chaotic behavior through the application of quantum entanglement, highlighting the advantages and challenges associated with this approach.

title: ## Big Free-tailed Bat Inspired Metaheuristic Algorithm for Complex Optimization Problems
abstract: This paper proposes a novel metaheuristic algorithm, termed the "Big Free-tailed Bat" (BFB) algorithm, inspired by the foraging behavior of the big free-tailed bat (Syracuseya brevicauda). These bats exhibit sophisticated strategies for locating food sources in complex and dynamic environments. The BFB algorithm leverages these strategies, specifically their echolocation and movement patterns, to address complex optimization problems. The algorithm employs a population-based approach, mimicking the bats' collective search process. Key components include a position representation based on bat location and flight direction, an energy function reflecting the success of a bat in finding food, and a communication mechanism inspired by bat social interactions. The algorithm incorporates a dynamic adjustment of flight direction and a probabilistic exploration strategy to avoid premature convergence. This paper details the theoretical framework, algorithm design, and a conceptual analysis of the BFB algorithm. We demonstrate its potential applicability across a range of optimization challenges, highlighting its adaptability and performance relative to established metaheuristic techniques. The algorithm's core mechanism relies on the following formulaic representations: `x_i(t) = x_i(t-1) + α * rand() * (x_best(t-1) - x_i(t-1))`, where `x_i(t)` is the position of the i-th bat at time t, `x_i(t-1)` is the position of the i-th bat at the previous time step, `x_best(t-1)` is the best position found so far, `α` is the learning rate, and `rand()` is a random number between 0 and 1. The energy function is defined as `E_i(t) = -log(fitness(x_i(t)))`, where `fitness(x_i(t))` represents the fitness of the i-th bat at time t. The algorithm's convergence is monitored through the tracking of the best fitness value: `f_best(t) = max{fitness(x_i(t)) | i = 1, 2, ..., N}`, where N is the population size. The algorithm's exploration strategy employs a probability distribution: `P(direction) = A * (1 - exp(-β * distance))`, where `A` is a scaling factor, `β` is a steepness parameter, and `distance` is the distance to the best solution.

We demonstrate its potential applicability across a range of optimization challenges, highlighting its adaptability and performance relative to established metaheuristic techniques. The algorithm's core mechanism relies on the following formulaic representations: `x_i(t) = x_i(t-1) + α * rand() * (x_best(t-1) - x_i(t-1))`, where `x_i(t)` is the position of the i-th bat at time t, `x_i(t-1)` is the position of the i-th bat at the previous time step, `x_best(t-1)` is the best position found so far, `α` is the learning rate, and `rand()` is a random number between 0 and 1. The energy function is defined as `E_i(t) = -log(fitness(x_i(t)))`, where `fitness(x_i(t))` represents the fitness of the i-th bat at time t. The algorithm's convergence is monitored through the tracking of the best fitness value: `f_best(t) = max{fitness(x_i(t)) | i = 1, 2, ..., N}`, where N is the population size. The algorithm's exploration strategy employs a probability distribution: `P(direction) = A * (1 - exp(-β * distance))`, where `A` is a scaling factor, `β` is a steepness parameter, and `distance` is the distance to the best solution.

title: Based on Evolutionary Algorithms for Hardware Design Optimization
abstract: This paper explores the application of evolutionary algorithms, specifically genetic algorithms, to the optimization of hardware design. The core claim is that evolutionary algorithms can effectively automate the process of enhancing both the performance and power consumption of hardware systems. The mechanism involves representing hardware design parameters as genes within a population, utilizing a genetic algorithm to drive iterative evolution, and employing selection, crossover, and mutation operators to refine the design. This approach offers a novel design methodology with the potential to significantly improve hardware efficiency. We present a framework for this approach and discuss its potential benefits and challenges. The focus is on the conceptual design and algorithmic foundations, without the need for experimental validation.

title: # Bear-Sloth: A Metaheuristic Algorithm Inspired by the Behavioral Patterns of Bears and Sloths
abstract: This paper introduces Bear-Sloth, a novel metaheuristic algorithm designed to address complex optimization problems. The algorithm's core inspiration stems from the unique behavioral patterns observed in bears and sloths – the bear's deliberate, methodical searching for food, and the sloth's slow, deliberate movement and clinging to trees. Bear-Sloth combines elements of Simulated Annealing (SA) and Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO) with a novel "Momentum-Adaptive Exploration" mechanism, mimicking the bear's foraging strategy and the sloth's stability. The algorithm incorporates a 'resting' phase, mirroring the sloth's inactivity, and a 'searching' phase, analogous to the bear's active searching. The performance of Bear-Sloth is evaluated on several benchmark optimization problems, demonstrating its effectiveness in finding near-optimal solutions with improved convergence speed and robustness compared to standard PSO and SA. Key features include adaptive inertia weights, a dynamically adjusted exploration rate, and a 'resting' phase to escape local optima. The algorithm's design aims for a balance between exploration and exploitation, leading to efficient optimization performance.

title: Title: Universal Quantum State Space Representation
abstract: Quantum state space representation is a fundamental challenge in quantum computing. The ability to represent quantum states in a manner that is both computationally efficient and invariant to rotations and translations is crucial for the development of quantum algorithms. This paper proposes a novel approach to defining a universal quantum state space, demonstrating its potential to facilitate the implementation of quantum algorithms across various measurement bases. The core mechanism centers on the creation of a generalized state space that inherently avoids these transformations, providing a robust foundation for algorithm transfer. We present a detailed explanation of the proposed representation, outlining its mathematical foundations and potential applications. The ultimate goal is to simplify the process of algorithm development and broaden the applicability of quantum computation.

title: Atlantic Forest Hocicudo: A Novel Metaheuristic Algorithm Inspired by the Hocicudo Animal
abstract: This paper presents Atlantic Forest Hocicudo (AFH), a novel metaheuristic algorithm inspired by the unique foraging behavior of the *Hocicudo* (a hypothetical animal adapted to the dense Atlantic Forest environment). The *Hocicudo*, characterized by its erratic movements, opportunistic feeding, and reliance on local environmental cues, serves as the foundation for AFH's design. AFH combines elements of Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO) and Artificial Bee Colony (ABC) algorithms, incorporating a novel "Adaptive Exploration-Exploitation" mechanism mimicking the *Hocicudo*'s behavior. The algorithm utilizes a dynamic population size, a stochastic movement strategy, and a local search operator based on environmental perception. Experimental results demonstrate that AFH outperforms several established metaheuristic algorithms, including PSO, ABC, and Genetic Algorithm (GA), on benchmark optimization problems. The key innovations of AFH lie in its adaptable exploration-exploitation balance and the incorporation of a localized perception mechanism. The algorithm's performance is evaluated across a range of problems, showcasing its effectiveness and adaptability. Future research will focus on refining the algorithm's parameters and exploring its application in more complex real-world scenarios.

The resulting framework promises to significantly enhance the rigor and speed of mathematical proofs. This is a significant advancement in probabilistic verification, offering a robust and potentially transformative approach to mathematical validation.

title: Quantum Entanglement-Driven Distributed Computing
abstract: This paper proposes a novel framework for distributed computing leveraging quantum entanglement, termed "Quantum Entanglement-Driven Distributed Computing" (QEDC). The core claim of this work is that utilizing quantum entanglement allows for the potential of superluminal information transfer and computation, effectively circumventing the communication bottlenecks inherent in classical distributed computing paradigms. The proposed mechanism involves constructing a distributed network composed of entangled qubits, exploiting the correlations within entangled states for parallel computation, and utilizing the instantaneous "collapse" of entangled states to achieve near-instantaneous information transmission. While acknowledging the theoretical challenges and the current limitations of quantum technology, this work lays out a foundational model for exploring this avenue, aiming to challenge existing computational models and potentially unlock new computational capabilities. The primary focus of this document is to outline the theoretical framework, key concepts, and potential implications of QEDC, without delving into experimental validation. The presented model explores the possibility of achieving computational advantages through the unique properties of entanglement, a concept that remains largely unexplored in the context of large-scale distributed computing systems. ---

title: ## The Deer-Inspired Adaptive Search Algorithm (DISA)
abstract: This paper introduces the Deer-Inspired Adaptive Search Algorithm (DISA), a novel metaheuristic optimization algorithm inspired by the foraging behavior of Japanese deer ( *Cervus nippon* ). Deer exhibit a sophisticated strategy for locating food resources, utilizing a combination of exploration and exploitation phases, influenced by environmental cues and herd dynamics. DISA mimics these behaviors through adaptive parameter adjustment, a dynamic population structure, and a weighted exploration-exploitation mechanism. The algorithm dynamically adjusts its search strategy based on the perceived "fitness" of the current solution set, prioritizing both exploration of new regions and exploitation of promising areas. This paper details the algorithm's design, its core principles, and presents a theoretical framework for understanding its convergence properties. The algorithm aims to provide a robust and efficient solution for a wide range of optimization problems.

title: ## The Chromatic Rhinoceros Optimization Algorithm (CROA)
abstract: This paper introduces the Chromatic Rhinoceros Optimization Algorithm (CROA), a novel metaheuristic algorithm inspired by the foraging behavior and color adaptation strategies of the Chromatic Rhinoceros, a unique avian species. CROA leverages the rhinocerous's ability to dynamically adjust its color camouflage for optimal survival in diverse environments, translating this into a robust search strategy for complex optimization problems. The algorithm utilizes a population of color-coded "rhinos," each represented by a vector of color values. Movement within the search space is driven by a color-matching mechanism mimicking the rhino's visual processing, combined with a polarization mechanism inspired by the animal's response to environmental changes. The core of CROA lies in its adaptive color-matching and polarization parameters, which are dynamically adjusted based on the landscape gradient and population diversity. This approach aims to provide a balance between exploration and exploitation, leading to efficient convergence and robust performance across a range of optimization challenges. This paper details the algorithm's theoretical foundation, design principles, and potential applications, laying the groundwork for future research and implementation.

abstract: This paper introduces the Kiwi-Inspired Metaheuristic Optimization Algorithm (KIMO), a novel metaheuristic algorithm inspired by the foraging strategies and navigational abilities of the New Zealand kākāpō (Kiwi parrot). This paper outlines the algorithm's theoretical framework, detailing the mathematical formulations governing its core components and emphasizing its potential applications in various optimization problems.

This research explores the potential of this approach to identify meaningful clusters and uncover hidden patterns within complex datasets. title: 基于动态的几何复杂度评估的优化算法
abstract: This paper introduces a novel optimization algorithm based on dynamic geometric complexity assessment. Traditional optimization algorithms often rely on static parameter settings, limiting their adaptability to varying input data. This work proposes a dynamic approach where the algorithm's optimization strategy is dynamically adjusted based on a measured geometric complexity of the input data. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this method through extensive experimental results, achieving significantly improved model accuracy and efficiency compared to existing optimization techniques. The core mechanism centers on continuously evaluating the complexity of the input during the optimization process, allowing for targeted adjustments to the algorithm's behavior. The paper also discusses the challenges and future directions of this approach.

title: Quantum States and Geometric Mapping for Quantum Computation
abstract: Quantum states, traditionally defined by their quantum numbers, possess a rich geometric structure that can be exploited to enhance quantum computation. This paper explores the concept of geometric mapping, a novel approach to represent and manipulate quantum states through geometric spaces. We investigate the potential of this technique to improve the efficiency and performance of quantum algorithms by optimizing quantum parameters within these geometric frameworks. The core claim is that exploring geometric mapping yields significant improvements in computational capabilities.

title: Social Media as an Alternative to Surveys of Opinions about the Economy
abstract: There is interest in using social media content to supplement or even substitute for survey data. O’Connor et al. (2010) report reasonably high correlations between the sentiment of tweets containing the word “jobs” and survey-based measures of consumer confidence in 2008-2009. Other researchers report a similar relationship through 2011 but after that time it is no longer observed, suggesting such tweets may not be as promising an alternative to survey responses as originally hoped. But, it’s possible that with the right analytic techniques, the sentiment of “jobs” tweets might still be an acceptable alternative. We explore this possibility by attempting to strengthen the original relationship and then extending the most successful approaches to more recent years. We classify “jobs” tweets into categories whose content is related to employment and categories whose content is not, to see if sentiment of the former correlates more highly with a survey-based measure of consumer sentiment. We use five sentiment-scoring tools, calculate daily sentiment three different ways, and use a measure of association less sensitive to outliers than correlation. None of these approaches improved the size of the relationship in the original or more recent data. We discuss the possibility that weighting and better understanding why users tweet might help recover the original relationship between the sentiment of tweets and survey responses. However, despite the earlier promise of tweets as an alternative to survey responses, we find no evidence that the original relationship was more than a chance occurrence.

title: A NEURAL NETWORK-BASED METHOD FOR EXTRACTING CAUSAL RELATIONS USING COMPARATIVE ANALYSIS OF SYNTHETIC AND OPEN CORPORA
abstract: Задача автоматического извлечения причинно-следственных связей (ПСС) критически важна для систем поддержки решений, но ее развитие сдерживается дефицитом размеченных корпусов. Цель исследования – сравнительный анализ эффективности трёх типов обучающих данных: открытых экспертных корпусов, реального политического корпуса с ручной разметкой и синтетических данных, генерируемых большой языковой моделью. Эксперименты выполнены на архитектуре DistilBERT с пословной разметкой по схеме BIOES. Синтетические данные генерировались LLM Llama-3 с инкапсуляцией причин и следствий в XML-маркеры и последующей детерминированной конвертацией в формат BIOES. Для сравнения использованы два экспертных корпуса (EventStoryLine, SemEval-2010 Task 8), экспертно размеченный политический корпус PolitiCAUSE и синтетическая выборка объёмом 1100 сбалансированных примеров. Модель, обученная на синтетических данных, достигла Macro F1 = 0,736, что на 6,7% выше результата модели, обученной на экспертных корпусах (0,690). Обучение на политическом корпусе PolitiCAUSE (24417 примеров) дало существенно более низкий результат - Macro F1 = 0,367. Данное расхождение обусловлено дисбалансом классов (около 15% каузальных токенов против 50% в синтетической выборке) и различием в постановке задачи: PolitiCAUSE ориентирован на бинарную классификацию наличия каузальности в предложении, тогда как в настоящей работе выполняется разметка спанов. Подтверждена гипотеза о приоритете качества и баланса аннотаций над объёмом данных. Предложенный пайплайн LLM-генерации позволяет создавать обучающие выборки, превосходящие по эффективности экспертные корпуса, при отсутствии прямых затрат на ручную аннотацию. Метод рекомендован для быстрого развёртывания систем извлечения каузальных отношений в новых предметных областях

title: The Privacy-Hallucination Tradeoff in Differentially Private Language Models
abstract: Both privacy and factual accuracy are paramount in high-stakes domains like healthcare. Concerningly, we uncover and investigate a privacy-hallucination tradeoff in differentially private (DP) language models. First, we empirically show that models pre-trained or fine-tuned with DP tend to produce more hallucinations than non-DP counterparts, with increased severity as the privacy budget grows stricter. Second, we investigate model properties driving this tradeoff, demonstrating that DP mechanisms flatten output distributions, potentially redistributing probability mass toward factually incorrect alternatives. Third, through experiments where we control fact frequency in training data, we characterize how information frequency can reduce hallucination risks in DP models. Overall, our findings underscore the need for more nuanced privacy-preserving interventions that offer rigorous privacy guarantees without compromising factual accuracy.

title: PauLie: Fast Classification of Pauli Dynamical Lie Algebras
abstract: The dynamical Lie algebra (DLA) governs the controllability, expressibility, and simulation complexity of a quantum system. Explicitly computing it has been a major computational bottleneck: brute-force Lie closure scales exponentially in the number of qubits $n$. Many applications, however, consult only the isomorphism type of the DLA. We introduce PauLie, an open-source framework that decides this isomorphism type for DLAs generated by arbitrary Pauli strings, building on the anticommutation-graph reduction of Aguilar et al. PauLie runs in $O(n|\mathcal{G}|\max(n,|\mathcal{G}|))$ time, where $|\mathcal{G}|$ is the number of generators, turning DLA classification into a routine preprocessing step. We demonstrate its use as a structural oracle for routing Lie-algebraic simulation and Cartan decomposition, diagnosing barren plateaus in variational quantum algorithms, and engineering universal Pauli string generator sets with optimal generation rate.

title: OPUS: A Simple yet Effective Unified Framework for Open-Vocabulary Detection
abstract: Recent unified open-vocabulary detection (OVD) supports heterogeneous prompts, including text queries, visual exemplars, and their combinations, but often rely on increasingly complex designs such as heavy cross-modal fusion, staged training, and iterative annotation pipelines. We revisit whether such complexity is necessary in the era of stronger foundation models. Our finding is that unified OVD can be made substantially simpler with semantic-rich visual representations and scalable grounding supervision. We present OPUS (Open-vocabulary, Prompt-Unified, Simple), a unified detector supporting text, interactive visual, generic visual, and mixed prompting within one framework. OPUS adopts a simple three-part design. Its model architecture combines a semantic-rich visual encoder, built on a DINOv3-ConvNeXt-B backbone with efficient hybrid encoding, with a prompt-aware decoder that avoids prompt-specific branches for unified prompt reasoning. OPUS is trained with a one-stage text-visual training strategy with Instance-level Contrastive Alignment (ICA), and is supported by a SAM3-based single-pass data engine for heterogeneous grounding supervision. Experiments on COCO, LVIS-minival, and ODinW35 show that OPUS achieves state-of-the-art Visual-I performance, reaching 68.1/69.2/54.7 AP, while maintaining balanced Text and Visual-G accuracy. OPUS also turns mixed prompting from interference into complementarity, improving over text or visual prompt alone. These results show that simplicity and strong unified prompting capability can be achieved together.

title: LLM-Based Knowledge Graph Completion Combining Discrete Structural Coding with Similar Entity Information
abstract: Knowledge graph completion requires models to use both textual descriptions and relational structure. Existing LLM-based methods either encode KG structure as discrete tokens or refine a restricted set of candidate entities, and these two directions have largely been studied separately. We propose CoSC for LLM-based KGC, which combines discrete structural coding with similar entity information. Specifically, an LLM generates an initial candidate entity ranking from discrete structural codes, after which information from entities with structures similar to that of the query entity refines the ranking. Experiments on FB15k-237 show that CoSC outperforms existing baselines on MRR and Hits@10 while remaining competitive on Hits@1.

title: Online Voting in Canada
abstract: The adoption of online voting in Canadian municipal elections raises fundamental questions about whether the infrastructure supporting democratic processes is held to an adequate security standard. This thesis presents a technical security analysis of the 2024 Nova Scotia municipal election, in which a single vendor served the overwhelming majority of the province's online-voting municipalities. Using publicly available observation tools, over 20 vulnerabilities were identified on active election infrastructure during the voting period. Most notably, a critical remote code execution flaw was found which was publicly known for more than a year before the election and was left unpatched throughout the election. These findings are evaluated against two independent audit documents and the CAN/DGSI 111-1:2024 national standard for online voting. Neither audit performed any technical assessment of the infrastructure. The DGSI standard, published after the election it would have governed, lacks meaningful provisions for patch enforcement and continuous vulnerability monitoring. A subsequent disclosure to the vendor confirmed that remediation was straightforward, suggesting that the prolonged exposure reflected absent accountability rather than technical infeasibility. This thesis maps observed vulnerabilities to concrete regulatory gaps and offers recommendations for vendors, administrators, and standard bodies. The central finding is that procedural compliance, without mandatory technical requirements and independent vendor oversight, provides little assurance that Canadian online election infrastructure is adequately protected.

title: Teaching the Colossus to Say No: A Historical Development Review of Alignment Strategies for Large Language Models
abstract: This article presents a narrative review of Alignment Strategies for Large Language Models in the context of Artificial Intelligence. The literature on this topic has expanded substantially over recent decades, yet it remains fragmented across subfields, methods, and national research traditions. Drawing on an interpretive synthesis of representative contributions, the review reconstructs the historical development of the area, examines the conceptual foundations and definitional disputes that organize its debates, and maps the contemporary landscape of research, including the methodological shift toward data-intensive approaches and the institutional pressures that shape publication practice. Particular attention is given to the role of alignment and large language models as organizing themes, and to the conditions under which findings from different research traditions can be brought into productive comparison. The review identifies three synthetic conclusions: the literature is cumulatively strong but organizationally weak; methodological pluralism is better understood as a resource than as a defect; and the growing practical salience of the topic raises the stakes of its unresolved conceptual questions. An agenda for future work is proposed, emphasizing integrative research designs, transparent synthesis practices, and the protection of definitional and infrastructural work on which cumulative progress depends. The article is intended as both a reference map for newcomers and a provocation for specialists in Artificial Intelligence.

title: The Voronoi of Data: A Narrative Review of K-Means Clustering, from MacQueen's Method to Careful Seeding and the Triangle Inequality
abstract: K-means is unsupervised learning's workhorse: partition the data by minimizing distances to means---an objective whose simplicity hides a hard optimization, a sensitive initialization, and a fifty-year engineering record. This article presents a narrative review of the primary literature of that workhorse. The synthesis is organized around three themes: the origins and convergence, in which Steinhaus's objective, Forgy's and MacQueen's methods, Lloyd's quantization algorithm, and Selim and Ismail's convergence theorem fixed the algorithm's mathematical frame; the efficiency and initialization era, in which BIRCH's summaries, Bradley's database scaling, Elkan's triangle-inequality pruning, Kanungo's analysis, and Arthur--Vassilvitskii's k-means++ seeding made the method scale and stabilized its starts; and the theory's extensions, in which Jain's fifty-year retrospective and Xing's metric learning reframed the question the means answer. It is concluded that k-means' history is the field's lesson in productive simplicity: an objective that everyone can state, an algorithm everyone can run, and a literature whose every paper---convergence, seeding, pruning, metrics---is the answer to one of the simple idea's hidden questions.

title: Non-Linear Matrix Quantum Computing and Geometric Transformations
abstract: This paper explores the potential of non-linear matrix quantum computing and geometric transformations for validating quantum matrix operations and establishing quantum algorithms. We investigate a novel framework leveraging the inherent properties of non-linear matrices to rigorously test quantum mechanical behaviors. The core mechanism centers on applying geometric transformations to matrix representations to reveal subtle quantum effects, ultimately leading to a more robust and adaptable validation method. The paper presents a preliminary analysis, showcasing the benefits of this approach compared to traditional quantum computing verification methods. The goal is to establish a foundational understanding of quantum matrix behavior through a combination of mathematical rigor and geometric manipulation.

title: Title: Dynamically Generated Modular Quantum Circuits
abstract: Quantum computing is rapidly advancing, driven by the need for scalable and adaptable architectures. Modular quantum circuits, where individual components can be combined and rearranged, offer a promising path towards this goal. This paper introduces a novel dynamic system for generating modular quantum circuits – the "Adaptive Circuit Generation" algorithm – which iteratively adds and removes modules based on input data, allowing for evolution and the creation of circuits capable of adapting to diverse conditions. This approach represents a significant departure from traditional static circuit design methods, providing a flexible and dynamic framework for quantum system development.

title: 基于自适应参数调整的联邦学习 (Adaptive Parameter Adjustment Federated Learning)
abstract: Federated Learning (FL) is a machine learning technique that enables training models on decentralized data sources while preserving data privacy. However, traditional FL approaches often rely on global model updates, which can be vulnerable to adversarial attacks and suboptimal performance on heterogeneous data. This paper proposes a novel framework called Adaptive Parameter Adjustment Federated Learning (APAFL) that dynamically adjusts model parameters based on local data characteristics, enhancing model robustness and privacy. We present a mechanism for adaptive parameter adjustment using a weighted aggregation of local model updates, mitigating the impact of noisy data and promoting better generalization. The proposed method demonstrates significant improvements in model accuracy and privacy compared to existing FL techniques.

title: Hierarchical Evolution of Topology in Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
abstract: This paper explores a novel approach to multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) by introducing an evolutionary mechanism focused on the hierarchical topology of agent connections. Traditional MARL primarily concentrates on optimizing individual agent policies, often neglecting the significant impact of the network structure on overall system performance. We propose a framework where agents dynamically evolve their communication topologies through reinforcement learning, guided by their collaborative outcomes. This evolution is driven by a competitive and cooperative process, allowing agents to adapt their connections to form a more efficient and robust network. The core claim is that by strategically evolving the topology, we can significantly improve the collaborative efficiency of multi-agent systems. The key mechanism involves agents exchanging information via communication and adjusting their connection topologies based on observed performance. This approach represents a shift from solely policy optimization to a holistic system-level optimization strategy. The proposed methodology offers a promising path towards designing truly adaptive and intelligent multi-agent systems.

title: Title: Cognitive Resonance Networks for Algorithmic Coherence
abstract: Cognitive Resonance Networks (CRNs) represent a promising paradigm for advancing neural network learning, particularly in the context of algorithmic coherence. This paper investigates the potential of leveraging cognitive resonance – the tendency for neural networks to converge on similar states – to enhance the stability and reliability of learning algorithms. We propose a novel attention mechanism that actively promotes the formation of these resonant states, fostering a feedback loop that encourages convergence. The core claim is that incorporating CRNs can mitigate instability and divergence, ultimately leading to improved algorithmic coherence. This work explores the theoretical implications of cognitive resonance and its practical implementation within neural network architectures. The paper will present a detailed analysis of the proposed attention mechanism and its impact on training dynamics, offering a framework for leveraging this phenomenon to improve the performance of various algorithmic tasks.

title: Information-Theoretic Analysis of Neural Network Dynamics
abstract: This paper investigates the dynamics of deep neural networks from an information-theoretic perspective. Traditional methods for analyzing neural network behavior often rely on gradient-based approaches or black-box testing, which can be insufficient for understanding the underlying mechanisms driving network evolution. We propose a novel framework utilizing entropy, mutual information, and related measures to quantify information flow within the network's activation space. This approach aims to identify critical information bottlenecks, assess the complexity of internal representations, and ultimately, contribute to the design of more efficient and robust neural network architectures. We demonstrate the application of these measures across several simplified network architectures, illustrating the potential for extracting meaningful insights into dynamic behavior. The core contribution lies in shifting the analytical focus from network output to the internal information processing, offering a new lens for understanding and controlling neural network dynamics.

title: Information Bottleneck Autoencoders for Anomaly Detection in Complex Systems
abstract: This paper investigates the application of information bottleneck autoencoders (IBAEs) for anomaly detection within complex systems. Traditional anomaly detection methods often struggle with the high dimensionality and intricate dependencies characteristic of these systems. The proposed approach leverages the information bottleneck principle to learn a compressed, informative representation of normal system behavior. By explicitly minimizing the mutual information between the input and the learned latent representation, the autoencoder is compelled to retain only the most salient features necessary for reconstruction, effectively highlighting deviations indicative of anomalies. We detail the architecture of the IBAEs, the training methodology, and the anomaly detection criteria. Through this framework, we demonstrate the potential of IBAEs to provide a robust and principled method for identifying anomalies in complex systems, offering a significant improvement over conventional techniques. The core claim centers around the use of the information bottleneck to identify anomalies, the core mechanism involves training an autoencoder for normal data reconstruction, and the novelty lies in applying this principle to complex systems for a principled approach to deviation detection.

title: Title: Dynamic Quantum State Collapse for Data Compression
abstract: This paper investigates the potential of dynamic quantum state collapse as a novel compression algorithm, aiming to surpass the current state-of-the-art in data compression rates through the strategic exploitation of quantum correlations inherent in data. We propose a 'Quantum State Collapse Engine' that dynamically collapses quantum states during the compression process, leveraging entanglement to represent data in a fundamentally more efficient manner. The core mechanism centers around quantifying and manipulating quantum entanglement to achieve superior compression ratios. This work presents a theoretical framework outlining the algorithm's design and potential performance improvements compared to existing compression techniques. We will detail the implementation of the Quantum State Collapse Engine and analyze its effectiveness through simulations, focusing on scenarios exhibiting strong quantum correlations. The goal is to demonstrate a substantial gain in compression rates, specifically for data containing significant quantum phenomena.

title: Algorithmic Complexity of Quantum Simulation of Complex Systems
abstract: Quantum simulation offers unprecedented capabilities for modeling complex quantum systems, but the inherent computational demands remain a significant obstacle. This paper investigates the algorithmic complexity of quantum simulation, specifically focusing on the development of a novel algorithm that harnesses quantum entanglement and superposition to dramatically reduce computational costs. We explore the challenges posed by the exponential scaling of classical simulations and propose a new approach based on a modified variational quantum eigensolver (VQE) framework, demonstrating a significant reduction in computational time for specific complex systems. The paper details the algorithm's design, the analysis of its complexity, and preliminary results demonstrating its effectiveness across a range of benchmark problems. The core claim is that this algorithm significantly advances the field by providing a pathway towards practical quantum simulations of increasingly complex systems, pushing the limits of computational complexity.

title: Quantum Machine Learning: A Feature Extraction Paradigm Leveraging Quantum Computing
abstract: Quantum Machine Learning (QML) promises a paradigm shift in artificial intelligence, offering the potential to overcome the limitations of classical computation. This paper explores the application of QML to feature extraction, specifically focusing on utilizing quantum algorithms to enhance data analysis and modeling. We propose a novel framework that transforms traditional machine learning models into quantum algorithms, capitalizing on quantum computing's unique properties, such as superposition and entanglement, to achieve significantly faster feature extraction and improved model performance. The core claim is that leveraging quantum computation for feature extraction can drastically increase the efficiency of machine learning algorithms, particularly in tasks involving complex data. This work investigates the potential of QML for image recognition, natural language processing, and other domains, demonstrating the feasibility of a quantum-enhanced feature extraction pipeline. The paper outlines the theoretical underpinnings of the proposed framework, discusses challenges and future directions, and provides a preliminary assessment of the potential impact of QML on these fields.

abstract: Quantum computing promises revolutionary advancements across diverse fields, but its current limitations stem from the complexities of quantum circuit design and optimization. abstract: This paper proposes a novel quantum computing architecture designed based on fundamental physical laws. We argue that by moving beyond the established paradigm of superconducting qubits, and embracing physically grounded approaches, we can significantly advance the performance and practicality of quantum computation. This document details the architectural components, outlines the key technological considerations, and presents a theoretical framework for a fundamentally robust quantum computing system. The focus is on building a system that aligns with known physical constraints, offering a more reliable path toward realizing the full potential of quantum computation. ---

title: Bearded Saki: A Metaheuristic Algorithm Inspired by the Behavior of *Crocodylus hirsutus*
abstract: This paper introduces a novel metaheuristic optimization algorithm, "Bearded Saki" (BS), inspired by the foraging behavior of *Crocodylus hirsutus*, commonly known as the Bearded Saki. These animals exhibit a unique strategy of alternating between short bursts of rapid movement and periods of stillness, effectively searching for food sources. BS leverages this dynamic behavior to construct a search space exploration strategy. The algorithm incorporates three key components: a "Stall" phase mimicking the Saki's stillness, a "Sprint" phase representing rapid movement, and a "Probe" phase for localized exploration. Mathematical formulations detailing the algorithm's core operations, including the probability calculation for transitioning between phases and the update mechanisms for solution parameters, are presented. The performance of BS is evaluated through a series of benchmark problems, demonstrating its efficacy in solving continuous optimization tasks. The algorithm's potential applications in various fields, including engineering design, financial modeling, and machine learning, are discussed. The results indicate that BS offers a competitive alternative to established metaheuristic methods, particularly in scenarios requiring adaptive exploration and exploitation.

title: Bare-backed Fruit Bat Inspired Metaheuristic Algorithm for Optimization Problems
abstract: This paper presents a novel metaheuristic algorithm, termed the "Bare-backed Fruit Bat Metaheuristic Algorithm" (BFFB), inspired by the foraging behavior of bare-backed fruit bats ( *Dilma fedosa*). These bats exhibit a unique exploratory-exploitative strategy, alternating between searching for new food sources and exploiting known, high-reward locations. The algorithm leverages this behavior to navigate complex optimization landscapes. BFFB incorporates a novel movement strategy based on the bat's flight patterns and a dynamic exploration-exploitation balance mechanism. The algorithm's core components include a position update rule, an attraction mechanism mimicking the bats' attraction to food sources, and an inertia term for smooth movement. The performance of BFFB is evaluated on a range of benchmark optimization problems, including the Sphere function, Rastrigin function, and Brent's patuitary function. The results demonstrate that BFFB achieves competitive performance compared to established metaheuristic algorithms such as the Artificial Bee Colony (ABC) and the Grey Wolf Optimizer (GWO), showcasing its potential as a robust and efficient solution for various optimization challenges. The algorithm's simplicity and adaptability make it a promising candidate for further development and application in diverse fields.

title: Distributed Program Evolution Based on Cellular Automata
abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to program evolution, termed Distributed Program Evolution Based on Cellular Automata (DPECA). The core idea is to leverage the inherent self-organizing behavior observed in biological cellular automata to facilitate the autonomous evolution and optimization of complex programs. The method decomposes program logic into a network of interacting cells, each responsible for executing a small portion of the overall program. These cells operate according to predefined rules, enabling the system to adapt and evolve without explicit human intervention. The theoretical framework utilizes concepts from cellular automata and evolutionary computation, aiming to provide a fundamentally new paradigm for program design. This approach seeks to overcome the limitations of traditional evolutionary algorithms by mimicking natural processes of self-organization and adaptation. The presented framework offers a potential pathway towards truly autonomous program development, particularly in scenarios demanding adaptability and resilience.

The core of this work lies in the development of a quantum algorithm specifically tailored for this task. This paper explores the potential of this framework for advancing the understanding and validation of fundamental mathematical concepts within the realm of topology.

abstract: This paper proposes a novel metaheuristic algorithm, Ashaninika Arboreal Chinchilla Rat (AACR), inspired by the foraging behavior of Ashaninika arboreal chinchillas. These rodents exhibit complex, hierarchical, and spatially organized foraging strategies within arboreal environments. AACR leverages these observed behaviors to develop a new optimization approach. The algorithm incorporates elements of particle swarm optimization (PSO), chimera optimization (CHO), and a novel representation of the search space based on tree structures, mimicking the chinchilla's spatial navigation and resource allocation. The core innovation lies in a dynamic tree structure that represents the potential solutions, allowing for efficient exploration and exploitation of the search space. The algorithm's performance is evaluated on a range of benchmark optimization problems, demonstrating its competitive capabilities and highlighting its potential for tackling complex, high-dimensional optimization challenges. title: Multi-Scale Cognitive Architecture
abstract: This paper proposes a novel multi-scale cognitive architecture designed to address the limitations of existing single-scale cognitive models. The core claim is that cognitive processes can be effectively decomposed into information processing occurring at multiple scales, necessitating a framework capable of simultaneously modeling both high-level cognitive structures and low-level neural activity. The proposed architecture utilizes a hierarchical structure with distinct layers dedicated to processing information at various scales. These layers are interconnected through feedback mechanisms, facilitating the integration and coordination required for complex cognitive operations. This approach represents a significant advancement over traditional cognitive architectures by offering a more comprehensive and realistic representation of cognitive processes. The architecture's key components, including scale-specific processing layers and feedback loops, are formally defined and described. The model aims to bridge the gap between cognitive theories and neuroscientific findings by providing a computational framework capable of capturing the dynamic interplay between different levels of analysis. Further research will focus on validating the architecture through simulations and exploring its potential applications in diverse cognitive domains.

title: Information Spread Networks in Simulated Ecosystems
abstract: This paper explores the emergent behaviors within simulated ecosystems by modeling information spread networks utilizing Agent-Based Modeling (ABM). The core concept involves simulating the exchange and competition of information carried by chemical signals (information素) between agents representing different species within a defined environment. The model incorporates diffusion dynamics of these signals, allowing for the investigation of complex interactions and potential optimization strategies. The research highlights the utility of ABM as a tool for understanding emergent phenomena in biological systems and its applicability to developing intelligent optimization algorithms. The model focuses on the dynamics of information flow, competition for resources, and the resulting population-level effects. Key parameters include agent movement, information素 concentration, and diffusion rates, which are dynamically adjusted within the simulation. The results demonstrate the potential for information素 networks to drive collective behavior and influence resource allocation in simulated ecosystems.

title: Aquatic Tenrec: A Novel Metaheuristic Algorithm Inspired by the Behavior of Aquatic Tenrecs
abstract: This paper presents Aquatic Tenrec, a novel metaheuristic algorithm inspired by the foraging behavior of aquatic tenrecs ( *Limnogale dichryptera*). Aquatic tenrecs are small, semi-aquatic mammals found in Madagascar that utilize a unique foraging strategy involving synchronized movement and a "wave-like" pattern to locate and capture prey. Aquatic Tenrec leverages this observed behavior to develop a new optimization algorithm designed for complex, multi-dimensional search spaces. The algorithm incorporates concepts of spatial coordination, dynamic adjustment of movement speed, and a distributed exploration strategy. We detail the algorithm's core components, including the generation of movement vectors, the synchronization mechanism, and the adjustment of parameters based on prey density. The algorithm's performance is evaluated through a series of benchmark problems, demonstrating its effectiveness in finding optimal or near-optimal solutions across various test functions. The results indicate that Aquatic Tenrec offers competitive performance compared to established metaheuristic algorithms such as Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO) and Artificial Bee Colony (ABC), particularly in scenarios requiring coordinated search strategies. Future work will explore the algorithm's adaptability to different problem domains and its integration with other optimization techniques.

title: The Arctic Ground Squirrel Metaheuristic Algorithm (AGSMA)
abstract: This paper introduces the Arctic Ground Squirrel Metaheuristic Algorithm (AGSMA), a novel metaheuristic optimization algorithm inspired by the foraging behavior of the Arctic ground squirrel ( *Urocitellus parvulus*). The algorithm leverages the squirrel's seasonal burrowing and food caching strategies to create a robust and efficient search process. AGSMA incorporates key elements such as a population-based search, a probabilistic selection mechanism mimicking the squirrel's preference for diverse food sources, and a dynamically adjusted exploration-exploitation balance. The algorithm's core mechanism, termed "Cache Intensity," represents the squirrel's level of resource utilization and is used to control the rate of solution diversification and intensification. This paper outlines the algorithm's design, detailing its parameters and operational rules. While lacking experimental validation, the theoretical framework and design principles are presented, laying the groundwork for future empirical testing and comparative analysis with established metaheuristic methods.

title: Computational Complexity Analysis of Quantum Algorithms using Randomized Benchmarking
abstract: The accurate determination of the computational complexity of quantum algorithms is a fundamental problem in quantum information science. Theoretical analysis often struggles to capture the subtle effects of noise and limited coherence, leading to inaccurate predictions. This work presents a rigorous methodology for assessing the complexity of quantum algorithms using randomized benchmarking (RB). RB provides a statistical framework for measuring the fidelity of quantum computations, allowing us to empirically estimate the number of gates, circuit depth, and other resource requirements. The approach avoids the pitfalls of purely theoretical models by directly observing the performance of a quantum circuit on a physical system. We demonstrate the application of this technique to several simplified quantum algorithms, illustrating the method's ability to provide more realistic estimates of complexity compared to traditional analytical approaches. The results highlight the importance of experimental validation in understanding the true resource demands of quantum computations.
